# Idle Speed Issues After Battery Replacement on a 2006 Toyota Camry

Replacing a battery in a 2006 Toyota Camry is a routine maintenance task, but if the engine idles too low, shudders violently, or stalls after the swap, it isn't necessarily a sign of a failing engine. The issue almost always stems from the Engine Control Module (ECM) losing its learned fuel trims and idle control data. When you disconnect the battery, even for just ten minutes, you interrupt the power supply to the ECM long enough to clear its volatile memory. This memory holds specific adaptation values that the computer has accumulated over thousands of miles to compensate for wear in the throttle body, variations in ignition timing, and changes in fuel pressure.

Once the new battery is connected, the system reboots with default factory settings. The idle speed control system is essentially "blind" until it can observe how the engine performs under current conditions. This process is known as relearning or re-adapting. During this phase, the ECM will cycle through different throttle plate positions and adjust the fuel delivery to find a stable operating point. If the engine shuts off while driving or idles in "limp mode" (a slow, unstable idle), it indicates that the adaptation values are still far from the optimal target.

While the user noted some improvement after 100 miles, the persistent shimmy suggests the relearning process is incomplete or interrupted. The ECM needs to see a variety of driving conditions to finalize these adaptations. A common practice to force this reset immediately is to disconnect the negative battery terminal again and then reconnect it without starting the engine. This ensures a hard reset of all stored adaptation data before the first drive cycle. Once the car is started, allow it to idle in neutral or park until the cooling fans kick on at least once. Do not touch the accelerator pedal during this initial warm-up period, as the computer needs to learn the baseline idle speed without user interference.

Driving characteristics are critical for the relearning process to complete successfully. The vehicle must be driven through a range of speeds and RPMs, including coming to a complete stop at traffic lights or in parking lots while in gear (not neutral). This allows the ECM to map out the relationship between throttle position and engine speed across different load conditions. If the car is only driven on highways where you never come to a full stop, the idle adaptation values may remain inaccurate because the computer never exercises the low-RPM control logic.

If the shuddering persists after a few days of mixed driving, inspect the throttle body for carbon buildup. A dirty throttle plate can restrict airflow, preventing the ECM from achieving the target idle speed even with correct adaptation values. Cleaning the throttle body and the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve is often a necessary step alongside the battery reset. There is no external screw or dial to manually adjust idle speed on this model; all adjustments are internal to the electronic control unit.

For developers managing embedded systems, this scenario highlights the importance of handling state persistence during power loss events. Just as an application might need to re-initialize a configuration cache after a reboot, an automotive ECU relies on learned parameters that must be recalibrated after a power interruption. The system is designed to eventually self-correct, but driver patience and specific driving patterns are required to guide the algorithm to convergence. If the problem continues after several days of varied driving and throttle body cleaning, professional diagnostics may be needed to rule out faulty sensors like the crankshaft position sensor or a failing IAC motor.
